subsystems.name: Bioink and matrix
subsystems.role: the printable material that becomes the tissue's scaffolding.

subsystems.name: Sacrificial ink
subsystems.role: a temporary material printed as the vessel network, later removed to leave hollow channels.

subsystems.name: Endothelial lining
subsystems.role: cells that coat the channels to make them blood-compatible.

subsystems.name: Bioprinter
subsystems.role: deposits multiple inks and cell types with micron precision.

subsystems.name: Perfusion bioreactor
subsystems.role: keeps channels open and supplies nutrients until implantation.

subsystems.name: Maturation and anastomosis
subsystems.role: grows the network into a stable tree and connects it to a host blood supply.

buildSteps.title: Design the vessel tree
buildSteps.detail: Software plans a branching network from a few millimetre-scale inlets down to capillaries tens of micrometres wide, so every cell sits within about 200 µm of a supply.

buildSteps.title: Prepare the bioink
buildSteps.detail: Organ cells are mixed into a warm hydrogel at low temperature to keep them alive and printable.

buildSteps.title: Print the sacrificial template
buildSteps.detail: The printer lays down the sacrificial ink in the shape of the vessel tree, sometimes co-axially with a gel sheath so each strand is a tube.

buildSteps.title: Cast or print the matrix
buildSteps.detail: The living bioink is printed around and over the template, locking the channels in place.

buildSteps.title: Dissolve the template
buildSteps.detail: Cooling, heating or a mild solvent removes the sacrificial ink, leaving an open, connected lumen.

buildSteps.title: Seed the endothelium
buildSteps.detail: Endothelial cells are flowed through the channels and stick to the walls, forming a non-clotting lining.

buildSteps.title: Perfuse and mature
buildSteps.detail: The construct sits in a bioreactor where medium is pumped through the network, feeding the tissue and training the vessels to stabilise.

buildSteps.title: Connect to a blood supply
buildSteps.detail: For implantation, the printed inlet is surgically joined to host vessels, or the tissue is placed where host capillaries grow in and fuse.

prerequisites.why: extrusion and light-based printers exist, but resolution and speed limit fine capillary networks.

prerequisites.tech: Hydrogel bioinks that set without killing cells
prerequisites.why: the material must be printable, non-toxic and strong enough to hold channels open.
the template must vanish completely without leaving residues that harm cells.
lining the channels is what stops blood clotting and keeps them alive.
without flow, tissue thicker than a fraction of a millimetre dies.
printed vessels must join the patient's own circulation without leaking or clotting.

pathway.milestone: centimetre-scale lab constructs with open, endothelial-lined channels kept alive for weeks
pathway.unlocks: proof that printed vessels can feed living tissue.

pathway.milestone: thick vascularised patches (e.g. cardiac or skin) tested in animals
pathway.unlocks: repair of damaged tissue without whole-organ replacement.

pathway.milestone: implantable organoids that connect to host blood supply and function
pathway.unlocks: treatments for organ failure using lab-grown tissue.

pathway.milestone: whole printed organs with a full vascular tree
pathway.unlocks: an alternative to donor waiting lists, if immune and long-term stability issues are solved.
